From here on, the second section clarifies the gathering of the multitudes from other directions to present offerings.
For what reason do those from other directions come to this place? Generally, there are three explanations: first, they come for their own sake, desiring to come to this location to make offerings.

Inviting the Dharma brings forth merit through making offerings; inviting the Dharma gives rise to wisdom. Therefore, the text below states: "Take this food and present it to that Buddha; you may also pay him homage and respectfully request a resolution to your doubts."
"Why did you not immediately make offerings and request the Dharma at the place where that Buddha resides, instead of coming here?
It is because of past affinities with this Buddha; as it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Puxing (Samantaprabha) came from afar, and so forth."
The second [category] consists of those who come for the sake of others; herein there are two types:
first, those who come for the sake of the sentient beings of this land, so that these beings may see them coming and thereby generate roots of goodness;

second, those who come for the sake of the sentient beings of that land, because the sentient beings of that land have prior karmic conditions with the Buddhas of this land and should see them to generate goodness, yet their power of virtue is weak and inferior such that they cannot move themselves, and thus those Bodhisattvas lead them here.

Therefore, within the section on the Bodhisattva Anantagātra below, it is stated that he sustains those immeasurable sentient beings and causes them to come here; this is the second reason for coming for the sake of others. Third, he comes as an influence and reflection to manifest the Dharma. In the text, it is proclaimed that immeasurable and boundless Anantagātras come from the four directions, with the eastern direction listed first; there are six distinct sections in the text: 1. First, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra of the east, together with his retinue, arrives at the place of the Buddha’s dwelling. 2. Second, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra of the south, together with his retinue, arrives at the place of the Buddha’s dwelling. 3. Third, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra of the west, together with his retinue, arrives at the place of the Buddha’s dwelling. 4. Fourth, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra of the north, together with his retinue, arrives at the place of the Buddha’s dwelling. 5. Fifth, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra of the southeast, together with his retinue, arrives at the place of the Buddha’s dwelling. 6. Sixth, the Bodhisattva Anantagātra of the southwest, together with his retinue, arrives at the place of the Buddha’s dwelling. The text states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantagātra of the eastern world-system, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who were his fellow practitioners, all adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics, arrived at the place where the Buddha was residing. This is the first section. The subsequent sections follow this same pattern. The text continues: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantagātra of the southern world-system, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who were his fellow practitioners, all adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics, arrived at the place where the Buddha was residing. First, listing the names of that land and its Buddha; second, manifesting that Buddha’s command for Anantagātra to come here; third, Anantagātra arriving here upon receiving the command; fourth, arriving and presenting offerings; fifth, the Tathāgata not accepting them; sixth, failing to achieve his purpose and remaining there.
Within the first section, the term "the eastern direction" indicates its location;
"immeasurable from here" reveals its distance;
and "the land named Abhirati" enumerates the name of that realm.
Below the phrase "The Buddha's name is Emptiness," the specific name of that Buddha is revealed.
"Emptiness" (ākāśa) is a specific name, while "Tathāgata," "Arhat," and so forth are general titles; all Buddhas possess these two types of names.
Because the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) must be distinguished, it is given a specific name;
because its actual qualities (*guṇa*) must be manifested, it is given a general designation.
There are ten such general designations, which will be explained in detail below.
In the second announcement, it first clarifies this land;
the passage beginning with "Therein dwells a Buddha" clarifies the Master of this transformation;
and the passage beginning with "He desires to enter parinirvāṇa; you should go" exhorts one to come and make offerings in order to generate merit.
The phrase "and may also pay homage" below encourages one to come and request the Dharma so that wisdom may arise.
Paying homage is the request through the body; requesting a resolution is the request through the mouth.

Thirdly, as for "coming here at the boundless command," he follows his transformation and comes from the east; yet in reality, he manifests within the equal Dharma-body, and is therefore said to "come."
Following the description of the lapis lazuli ground below, the emission of light should be understood accordingly.
Now, regarding the characteristics of the transformation, there are nine distinct sections in the text:
first, paying respectful homage to that Buddha and expressing the desire to come here;
First, two [beings] came to this place and first manifested auspicious signs;
second, those at this place were startled and terrified upon seeing the signs; third, Mañjuśrī comforted them; and fourth, [the account of their subsequent transformation].
Five: It is explained that this assembly sought him by following his words and thus beheld him;
Six: Mañjuśrī informed the assembly, "By the power of the Buddha, you shall behold him in the nine directions";
Seven: It is explained that once the great assembly knew he had already come and that the Tathāgata was certainly about to enter parinirvāṇa, they all sighed with grief.
Eighth, it clarifies that the great assembly witnessed his miraculous transformations through the majestic power of Anantagātra;
ninth, it clarifies that the dimensions and limits of Anantagātra’s body can be seen only by a Buddha, and cannot be seen by others.
The first section begins with "Anantagātra immediately received the instruction," and so forth.
The second section begins with "At that time, this... and so on.
Regarding the "six kinds of movements," as described in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, they are: shaking, surging, trembling, awakening, roaring, and rising.
The section beginning with "At that time, the assembly... constitutes the third part, clarifying the astonishment and fear of the assembly.
Why is it so? Because the majesty and dignity of this Bodhisattva are so profound as to be truly terrifying; thus, he causes the assembly to be afraid.
Furthermore, since his arrival, the Tathāgata has certainly entered parinirvāṇa and great suffering is about to come; because the facts and principles are thus, they cause the multitude to fear.
When the Vaiśālī king came down [to the city], why was it not so?

He has come to reveal the true meaning so that people may realize and enter it, and furthermore, he wishes to guide others toward rebirth in the Pure Land; as this supreme benefit is about to arrive, he causes the assembly to rejoice.

Ananda has now arrived, but the minds of the assembly are not yet unified; to increase their longing and veneration, he caused them to feel startled and fearful. Transformation adapts to the occasion and cannot be fixed.

The section beginning with "At that time Mañjuśrī" constitutes the fourth segment. Mañjuśrī offers consolation: first, he exhorts [the audience] not to fear; the section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation; and the section beginning with "Therefore" provides the conclusion.
The section beginning with "At that time, the great assembly all saw from afar" constitutes the fifth segment; it describes seeing them immediately upon speaking.

The section beginning with "Mañjuśrī further addressed" constitutes the sixth segment; it is Mañjuśrī’s prophetic declaration, clarifying that by the power of the Buddha, they shall see [the Buddhas] in the nine directions.
Where can they be seen?

They are seen within the transformed lands of the Tathāgatas below; there, one sees the Buddha-lands of the ten directions in general, not merely the boundless places from which [beings] come, for those boundless places of origin exist only in the four cardinal directions.

The section beginning with "At that time, the great assembly spoke to one another" constitutes the seventh segment; the assembly laments and sighs, saying, "Since the Great Being has arrived, the passing of the Sage is not far off," and thus they mourn the emptiness of the world.

The section beginning with “At that time, the entire great assembly” constitutes the eighth segment, clarifying how the multitude witnessed his supernormal transformations through his boundless power. This contains two parts:
first, witnessing his supernormal transformations; second, from “By means of this bodhisattva’s power of supernatural penetration,” which clarifies the cause and conditions for such witnessing.
The preceding section has three parts:

first, seeing his own body along with his retinue; second, from the phrase "each and every pore" downward, seeing the lands, people, and inhabitants within his body; third, from the phrase "at that time, surrounded by boundless and immeasurable bodhisattvas" downward, seeing the articles of offering he holds.
The first section may be understood as it stands.
In the second section, first one sees the lands; from the passage "In each of these cities there are eighty-four thousand kings" onwards, one sees the people, which contains three parts:
first, seeing them enjoying pleasure; second, from "Among them" onwards, seeing them practicing virtue; and third, from "Dwelling in peace" onwards, seeing their lamentation.
At the beginning and middle [of this section], one first sees the human kings enjoying happiness and subsequently sees the common people; the meaning is clear and can be understood from the text.
Within the description of seeing those who practice goodness, the first part clarifies what they hear—exclusively hearing the Mahāyāna;
the passage beginning with "Within each flower is a lion throne" clarifies what they preach—exclusively preaching the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the phrase "Its robes are subtle and transcend the three realms," this means that as a pure retribution of the supramundane, they surpass the three realms.
The passage beginning with "Or there may be sentient beings who copy and uphold [this]" clarifies what they practice: they exclusively cultivate the Mahāyāna.

Within the passage on "seeing and lamenting the injuries," the phrase "having already established oneself in the immeasurable" cites what preceded to introduce what follows, thereby causing one to relinquish worldly pleasures and give rise to a mind of revulsion.
"All say the world is empty," they said, which increased their feelings of attachment; longing for the Sage and fearing his extinction, they spoke words of lamentation.
Is the view held by these people true?
Is it a transformation?
Śāriputra replied:
It must be real.
If this is true, for what reason does he dwell within the body of the Boundless One?
The explanation is:
the relationship between the body and the land is not fixed; sometimes the body relies upon the land, as is commonly seen.

Alternatively, the land may depend upon the body, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "The bases upon which the lands of all Buddhas rest are not fixed; they may abide within the celestial crowns of Bodhisattvas, or abide within the folds of the robes of Bodhisattvas, or abide within the palms of the Māṇibhadra spirits, or abide by virtue of the power of Samantabhadra’s vows."
"Now, it is not at all strange that he dwells within infinite pores.
The preceding section was the second: seeing the lands and the people within his body.
From here on is the third: seeing the offerings he holds.
"At that time, after Anantaprabhāsa had manifested his supernormal powers," this phrase recapitulates what preceded and introduces what follows.

Below, the offerings are explained; first, the matters of incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and so forth are addressed. "Various" means many; "immeasurable" means vast, signifying that each individual type is itself immeasurable.
The following clarifies that his food and drink are supremely sublime; this refers to the excellence of the substance of his fragrant and delicious meals.
If one hears that his defilements have been extinguished, this refers to the excellence of his provisions.
Thus far, the first section has shown his supernormal transformations.

The section beginning with "By means of this bodhisattva’s supernormal power" constitutes the second segment, which concludes by clarifying the reason why the great assembly is able to see [the Buddha].

From the point where it says "The assembly all saw the Boundless Body" onwards, these are combined as the eighth [section]. From here on, the ninth section clarifies the limits of that Boundless Body's dimensions: it is visible only to the Buddha, while others cannot see it.

Regarding the phrase "the body is vast and boundless, its measure equal to space," this refers to a Buddha whose measure is equal to the space of that realm; it may also be equal to the space of the *dharmatā*.

Hitherto, the great assembly has perceived only this transformation; in reality, it is vast and expansive. Just as the Dharma-body of all Buddhas of the three periods throughout the dharma-realm is identical, it is known only by the Buddhas themselves, while others are unable to see it.
The Bodhisattva Samantagāmin should also have seen this, but it is not discussed here in detail.
The preceding nine sections together constitute the third part, "Receiving the Command and Coming Here.
The fourth section, "Presenting Offerings," the fifth, "Not Accepting," and the sixth, "Withdrawing and Remaining," are clear and can be understood from the text.
Below, the text explains that the Bodhisattva Anantagātra comes from other directions, manifesting his place of origin from the south, west, and north.

The phrase "there are also immeasurable and boundless bodies" distinguishes and enumerates these individuals; it means that in each direction there are immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas named Anantagātra who come together to present offerings, rather than meaning that only one such person comes from each direction.

Regarding the phrase "double the previous": that which is provided in the south exceeds what was set out in the east and what was previously offered; this continues until that which is provided in the north exceeds what was set out and offered in the three directions without limit. Because he rejects the invitation and does not accept it, remaining aloof and standing apart, it is said "up to" (乃至).
From here below is the eighth section, which summarizes the assembly; it contains four parts:

first, to clarify the extent of the gathering of the śāla trees—within an area thirty-two yojanas in length and breadth, the great assembly is fully present—and that this place gives rise to goodness, thus it is named the Auspicious Ground (Śrībhūmi).
One *yojana* consists of forty *li*; thirty-two *yojanas* thus total one thousand two hundred and eighty *li*, which are entirely filled.

Why is it that the area of twelve *yojanas* in the center where the previous lay devotee adorned [the site], the thirty-two *yojanas* within this [area], and the forty *yojanas* beneath the lion throne are not equal?
This is because it corresponds to the three extensive abodes; thus, it is the same as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Second, from "At that time, the Boundless Body from the four directions" onwards, the text explains the prevention of doubts and difficulties.
What is the nature of this doubt?

The body of Anantagātra is vast, measuring thirty-two *yojanas* in height; since that location is so extremely narrow, how could they accommodate one another, let alone admit the rest of the assembly?

Therefore, I shall now explain this: since the four directions are boundless, the space occupied by those seated may be as small as the point of an awl, the tip of a needle, or a speck of dust; thus, they are able to accommodate one another.
Many people say that the boundless bodies from the ten directions have come; however, judging by the preceding evidence, there are only four directions.

Third, from "the ten directions" downward, it clarifies that the assembly has gathered; therein, it first clarifies the gathering of the assembly from other regions, which consists solely of bodhisattvas.

The phrase "and those from Jambudvīpa" indicates that the assembly of this region has gathered; various classes of beings have all assembled. First, the gathering of humans is clarified, excluding Kāśyapa and others; the section beginning with "down to" indicates that the remaining multitude has all assembled.

The sixteen types of evil conduct are as explained below in the "Siṃha-parivarta" (Lion Chapter); the four "Dānavas" below clarify that the assembled multitude all abandoned their evil thoughts and looked upon one another with hearts of loving-kindness.
Within this, first is the principle, next is the analogy, and finally is the application; below this, the icchantikas are excluded.
From here on, the ninth section concerns the transformation of the land to make it pure.
"The trichiliocosm" refers to the extent of that purity.
"By the Buddha's spiritual power" indicates the source by which the land is purified.
"The ground is entirely soft," and so forth, correctly clarifies the purity of the land.
"Just as in the Western [Pure Land]" serves as an analogy to manifest the characteristics of that purity.
That land is eternally pure.

Beings originally perceive it as defiled because of their prior unwholesome states of mind; through the Buddha’s power, these are transformed, and only now do they see its purity. This is called "transforming the land," but in principle, it is actually the transformation of the mind.

From here on is the tenth section, clarifying how the great assembly, due to the purity of the land, perceives throughout the ten directions lands as numerous as motes of dust; herein, first is the teaching, next is the simile, and finally is the application.
Mañjuśrī spoke first, saying, "By the power of the Buddha, you shall see the nine directions," referring to this very matter.
Since these are the ten directions, for what reason does he speak of nine?
When the former [light] was announced, the eastern direction had already been seen; because this refers to what was seen there, it specifically mentions "nine.
In the eleventh section below, when the Tathāgata’s transformation is complete, he gathers the light back into his mouth.
Previously, six rays of light were emitted; for what reason is it said there are five?
This is explained as above: crystal and agate are combined to form variegated colors, and for this reason, five are mentioned.
Furthermore, foreign scholars traditionally explain that among the six rays emitted, one was retained to transmit the Dharma; therefore, only five were gathered.
While the previous [rays] illuminated the ten directions, why is it said here that they only "cover the assembly"?

This is also explained as above: it is because [the light] follows those sentient beings whom it illuminates; since the demonstration of transformation has been completed, [the light] enters through the mouth.
The twelfth section below clarifies how the great assembly beheld this sign and was moved by grief and distress;
herein there are four parts: first, beholding the sign with alarm and fear: "Seeing the light enter the mouth, they were all greatly terrified"—this refers to the shock within their hearts.
1. "The hairs on his body all stood on end" indicates that his physical form was ill at ease.
2. From "He further spoke" onwards, it distinguishes how the light entered his mind.
3. From "How could I have expected" onwards, he speaks words of lamentation and sorrow.
There are four kinds of injury:
first, the injury already suffered, which brings present grief and affliction; second, the suffering of falling into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Fearing that these will suddenly arrive, one asks, "How could this be? (何期).
The particle "zai" (哉) expresses the utmost resentment and lamentation, used as a reduplicated exclamation.

Regarding the two instances of "once upon a time" (yī dàn): the following passages express grief over not receiving offerings; [the Buddha] formerly practiced the four immeasurables to benefit the world, yet now he abandons that name and ceases those deeds.
The "four immeasurable minds" are explained in detail below.
Not accepting offerings is the characteristic of relinquishment.

Third, "the eternal cessation through noble wisdom": this expresses grief at the loss of the Teacher. Noble wisdom dispels darkness, like the sun or the moon; therefore, it is named after these metaphors.
4. "The Dharma-ship Sinks": Lamenting that the Dharma will perish prematurely; for the Dharma can ferry beings across, it is metaphorically called a "ship. This concludes the third section. 4.
From "Alas" (*aho*) onwards, there is grief, resentment, and anguish; the intensity of this sorrow increases, and blood flows, drenching the earth.
This concludes the introductory section.
Regarding the second part of the sutra,
the "Section on Opening the Doctrine and Revealing Virtue," it first recounts divergent views, next discriminates between what is correct and incorrect, and finally reveals the true meaning.
What are these alternative theories?

Traditionally, it has been transmitted that from this point up to the subsequent "Kāśyapa-parivarta" constitutes the orthodox canon (*saddharma*). Within this orthodox canon, there are two broad divisions and six detailed subdivisions.

The coarse classification into two parts consists solely of the brief and the extensive: from the beginning up to the "Chapter on the Multitude" (Zongpin) is the brief exposition, while from the "Chapter on the Multitude" onwards is the extensive exposition.
Regarding the sixfold subdivision, there are briefly three parts:

first, clarifying the manifested fruit of the Buddha; second, from "The Three Announcements" onwards, revealing its conditional causes; and third, from "In the twenty-five states of existence, is there a self? onwards, manifesting the true cause of the Buddha-nature.
The extensive version also has three parts:

first, the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly" extensively explains the previously mentioned manifest fruit; second, from the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" onwards, it extensively explains the aforementioned conditional causes; third, from the "Lion Chapter" onwards, it extensively explains the previously mentioned direct cause. Such are the differing interpretations.
Next, the merits and faults are distinguished.
What has been transmitted since antiquity appears correct at first glance, yet upon minute investigation, it is not so.
This shall be analyzed through two points:
First, one must verify by comparing the questions; second, one must seek the meaning within the text itself.

Regarding verification by comparison: if the sections before and after the "Chapter on the Multitude" differ in their brevity or detail, then they ought to be questioned and answered separately at both locations. For what reason, then, would a question from the brief version be paired with an answer from the extensive version, or a question from the extensive text be paired with an answer from the brief version?
However, from "The Three Announcements" onwards, Kāśyapa asks extensively and the Tathāgata answers extensively.
Is it not a distortion to abruptly divide this extensive answer midway, making the first part concise and the latter part extensive?

From "The Three Announcements" (*sāngào*) onwards, the questions and answers are presented together to clarify that this constitutes a single section, rather than being a separate extensive or abbreviated portion.

Furthermore, if there were six sections and these were to be explained in sequential order, then [the questions] should have been posed together at the beginning of the "Cunda Chapter" (*Chuntuó zhāng*), followed by the answers; they should not have waited until after the "Lamentation Chapter" (*Āitàn zhāng*) for Cunda to pose his questions. Since the questions and answers are provided separately after both the "Cunda" and "Lamentation" chapters, it is clear that this section is entirely distinct from the preceding ones and cannot be combined with them to form six sections.

If the sections on "Cunda" and "Lamentation" were distinct from the subsequent meaning, they could not have been asked about and answered together in one place; rather, it is after the "Three Announcements" that they are asked about and answered together, clarifying that they constitute a single part and cannot be combined with the preceding material to form six parts.
The inquiry is thus.
Next, one must examine its correctness based on the text itself.

Within the six divisions previously established, the first clearly elucidates the fruition, while the second division distinguishes and clarifies the causal conditions; this is the general outline of their characteristics.

If it is claimed that from the passage "the twenty-five realms of existence" down to the subsequent "Chapter on the Multitude," all sections collectively clarify the Buddha-nature as the direct cause,
this interpretation is incorrect.
As clarified below in the exposition of the Bodhisattva, one perceives the difficulty and perceives the nature, thereby understanding the "half" and "full" meanings of the word *bodhisattva*.

Even one who has not yet resolved to attain enlightenment may be called a Bodhisattva; they possess fearlessness among the multitude, remain unstained by the turbid world like a lotus flower, and dwell amidst afflictions without being defiled by them. Observing the Triple Gem, they attain an assembly that cannot be destroyed, acting as eyes and guides for all those born blind.
These answers to the nine questions all clarify the bodhisattva’s practice as the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
How, then, can it be called the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*)?

Furthermore, as explained below: the Tathāgata manifests transformations; like the *kālaṃjara* bird; like the sun, moon, and Jupiter; the Buddha acts as a boatman; the Buddha abandons birth and death; like a snake shedding its skin; the Buddha displays many heads; and his teaching is like the crescent moon.
These answers to the eight questions all clarify the Tathāgata’s manifest karmic functions.
How, then, can they be called the "correct cause" (samyag-hetu) of Buddha-nature?
Another person further explains, saying:
"Although this meaning has been distinguished, the primary thesis reveals the Buddha-nature; therefore, it is called the 'True Cause' (zhengyin).
Since the text does not explicitly state this, how can it be known?
That such a vast amount of scriptural text exclusively reveals the Buddha-nature is a great difficulty to understand."

Furthermore, if these [sections] do not actually discuss nature (*svabhāva*) but rather manifest it, then the "Cunda" and "Lamentation" chapters—which do not actually distinguish causes—should be called "Manifesting Causes.
Similarly, from the "Three Announcements" onwards—which do not actually speak of results—should be called "Manifesting Results."
However, where the fruit is spoken of, it cannot be called the cause; where the cause is spoken of, it cannot be called the fruit.
Since their intrinsic nature is not spoken of in those instances, how can one insistently compel them to speak of that nature?
It is truly because people of the world do not understand its textual structure that they have recklessly made this judgment; the great error lies in this sixfold division of the text.
People say: "The 'Chapter on the Multitude' expands upon the previously mentioned manifest results."
This is also not the case. Why is it not the case?

In the lower section, the "Chapter on the Multitude," the seven questions are answered in full; the answer to the first question clarifies that the Buddha is eternally abiding, which may be designated as the "fruit."
Answer: The latter six questions all clarify causal practice; how, then, can they be said to expand upon the previously manifested results?
Furthermore, it is stated:
"The two chapters, 'Simha' and 'Kāśyapa,' expand upon the previously mentioned correct cause."

This is also not the case; according to the subsequent questions and answers, it is in the later *Kāśyapa-parivarta* that the Tathāgata’s skillful application of his virtues and functions in benefiting even icchantikas is clarified, rather than for the purpose of revealing the [Buddha-]nature. How, then, can this be called an expansion of the aforementioned correct cause?
Seeking the truth through these evidences, it is certain that the sixfold division is incorrect.
Next, the correct principle shall be revealed.
This sutra consists of five distinct sections from beginning to end, as fully determined in the preceding analysis.
The preceding section constitutes the Introduction;
this current portion, the "Utterly Lamenting," is the second section, which opens the doctrine and manifests its virtues;
from "The Three Announcements" onwards is the third section, which distinguishes the virtues accomplished through cultivation.
"If one can know this, they are called a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa"—the following constitutes the fourth section, which refutes heterodoxy and establishes the correct [teaching].
The fifth section concerns the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa: the great assembly of humans and devas performed the cremation and made offerings, while those from foreign lands did not come.

Among these five [sections], the first concerns the skillful means for converting and benefiting others; the middle three concern the actual conversion and benefit; and the final portion concerns entering parinirvāṇa once the conversion is complete.
Within the middle three sections concerning the actual conversion and benefit, there are three types of those benefited, four distinct textual divisions, and six detailed subdivisions.
The three ways of benefiting others are: benefiting ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), *śrāvakas*, and *bodhisattvas*; these are the three. Regarding the four distinct textual sections:

from the beginning up until the parable of the stars, the text benefits *śrāvakas* by causing them to study the Mahāyāna; therefore, in the subsequent passages, it frequently clarifies how the Tathāgata causes them to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and return to the Great Vehicle.

Second, from the passage "Just as when the sun rises, the mists are dispelled" onwards, it benefits ordinary persons by causing them to enter the Buddha-dharma; therefore, in the subsequent passages, it frequently clarifies how it benefits the three types of offenders and others, leading them to enter the Buddha-dharma.
From the third chapter, "Noble Practices" (Ārya-caryā), onwards, the text benefits bodhisattvas; therefore, the subsequent sections exclusively clarify what bodhisattvas cultivate and realize.

From the fourth chapter, "Kāśyapa," down to the "Cunda" chapter, the text benefits ordinary beings; therefore, the subsequent sections clarify the conversion of icchantikas, various māras, and non-Buddhists, leading them to enter the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the sixfold subdivision: within the second [section] above, the characteristics are further divided into two.

From the beginning up to the end of the "Mahāparipṛcchā-parivarta," it primarily clarifies the transformation and benefit of ordinary beings with transgressions, causing them to leave the three types of offenses and enter the Buddha-dharma;

the single chapter "Vyādhisamdarśana" primarily clarifies the transformation and benefit of ordinary beings suffering from pain, manifesting supernatural powers and preaching the Dharma to cause them to leave suffering.
The fourth section, which further clarifies the benefits of transformation among ordinary beings, also has two distinct parts:
first, the "Kāśyapa Chapter" clarifies the transformation of icchantikas, causing them to believe in the Buddha-dharma;
second, within the "Cundabhadrī Chapter," there is the transformation of Māras and non-Buddhists, causing them to return to the Buddha-dharma.
In other comprehensive expositions, six sections are taught;
the middle three sections benefit people in this manner.

Within the first section, which opens the doctrine and reveals its virtues, it is explained through four propositions, the first of which defines the meaning of opening the doctrine and revealing its virtues.
The "Essential Principle" (zong) refers to the eternal fruit, which is opened in two ways:
first, by sweeping away the provisional to reveal the true, which is called "opening"; second, by refuting the Lesser Vehicle to reveal the Great Vehicle, which is called "opening.
In the "Chapter on Cunda," the sweeping away of the provisional to reveal the true is termed "opening the Essential Principle."
In the "Chapter on Sighing" (*Aishan-zhang*), the refutation of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to reveal the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) is termed the "opening of the school.

This is because the eternal principle (*nitya-tattva*) was formerly obscured by the traces of the teaching on impermanence (*anityatā*); thus, it was necessary to sweep away the provisional response to reveal the true reality and thereby open [the path].
Furthermore, as it was formerly covered by the verbal traces of the Small Vehicle, it was necessary to refute the Small Vehicle to reveal the Great Vehicle and thereby open [the path].
Second, distinguishing [the categories] with respect to persons.
There are two kinds of persons:
first, those who serve as the locus of entrustment; second, those for whose sake [the teaching is given].
The one upon whom they rely is the Buddha; the ones for whom he acts are sentient beings.

These sentient beings possess a permanent nature within their bodies, yet it is obscured by delusions and hindrances such that they do not perceive it. It is like a poor woman who has a treasure storehouse within her house but is unable to know of its existence; she now wishes to forget it, yet [the Buddha] desires to manifest the truth so that they may enter it. However, because the true principle is difficult to reveal through the mere analysis of delusion, he relies upon the Buddha to open it up.
Although it is said that the Buddha is eternal, the underlying intent is to reveal that the bodies of sentient beings possess an eternal nature, thereby leading them to enter [the path].
Third, distinguishing [the teachings] according to the persons addressed: there are two types of persons.
The first are those addressed by the transformation of the Sage, namely the class of "echoes" (yǐngxiǎng) and so forth.
The two sages’ transformative activities were directed toward those who were ready to receive the teaching.
Pureṇa and Mañjuśrī served as their echoes and influences, while the various bhikṣus and others who were training in impermanence were the ones upon whom these activities were performed.

Because their wisdom was inferior, they were unable to inquire about or clarify the meaning of the eternal beyond the conventional; therefore, in the "Chapter on Cunda," I first revealed the eternal Dharma in response to their influence.

Because the preceding section opened the fundamental tenets, the bhikṣus and others were gradually able to awaken to and enter into the meaning of the "constant dharma" (dharmatā); therefore, in the following "Lamentation" chapter, the text provides an extensive explanation of the meaning of the "constant" in response to their practice.
The commentary on the *Caturvarga-vinaya* explains that in the "Chapter on Cunda," the permanence of the Tathāgata’s fruition of bodhi is revealed;
in the "Chapter on Lamentation," the permanence of the Tathāgata’s dharma-nirvāṇa is made manifest through his deeds.
What is the difference between these two such that they must be discussed separately?

In general explanation, they are one: all virtues characterized by stillness are called *nirvāṇa*, and all that is empty, pervasive, and unimpeded is called *bodhi*. While there is no lack of distinction when categorized according to their specific characteristics, they are fundamentally one.

There are three kinds of distinctions: First, the distinction between cause and fruit: the cause is termed *bodhi* (enlightenment); since *bodhi* is the Path, all that is practiced within the causal stage—leading through the human realm to the fruit—is collectively called the "Path. The fruit is termed *nirvāṇa* (extinction); since *nirvāṇa* is cessation, upon reaching the fruit one abandons cultivation; being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and tranquil, it is collectively called "Cessation.

Second, the distinction between the abandonment of practice and the attainment of virtue: all virtues of practice are termed *bodhi*, while all virtues of abandonment are uniformly designated as *nirvāṇa*.

Third, regarding the distinct discussion of the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and skillful means (*upāya*): as stated in the subsequent text, "The fruits of skillful means arising from the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*) are all termed *bodhi*, while the fruit of the purity of nature revealed by the revealing cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*) is called *nirvāṇa*. Now, following the latter category, the retribution of skillful means is coarse, whereas the dharma of the purity of nature is subtle; therefore, it is discussed later.
Question: This sutra takes *nirvāṇa* as its central theme; for what reason, then, is *bodhi* being expounded here? Answer:
It is explained as follows:
From the perspective of distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the two gates of bodhi and nirvāṇa are separate;
however, according to the perspective of inclusive characteristics (*saṃgraha-lakṣaṇa*), they mutually support one another.
Now, based on the perspective of inclusive characteristics, it is said that bodhisattvas also realize nirvāṇa; thus, this sutra fully elucidates both bodhi and nirvāṇa as the eternal fruit.
Regarding the title of this sutra, which states "Mahāparinirvāṇa," this name refers to the dharma of inexhaustibility; it merely cites one aspect and does not state it in its entirety.
Within the "Cunda Chapter," there are two meanings and three textual sections.

Regarding the two meanings: first, it clarifies that the Tathāgata’s true body (*dharmakāya*) is eternally abiding; second, it clarifies that the Tathāgata’s manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is impermanent. Question:

The true eternity has been concealed since antiquity and may now be revealed; however, the manifested body is an old transformation that has been constantly seen since time immemorial—why is it necessary to speak of it?
The commentary states:

Although the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is an ancient manifestation, what was previously spoken was the truth, while what is now being discussed is the response; therefore, it must be distinguished.
Furthermore, because provisional means may be concealed, guided, or even withdrawn, it is necessary to clarify the nature of the response.
The text clarifies that the Buddha is truly eternal, desiring to lead sentient beings to enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
it reveals that the Buddha appears to pass into extinction, in order to cause sentient beings to likewise grow weary of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
As for the three distinct sections: first, the Buddha addresses Cunda to distinguish between the true and the manifested.
2. From "Cunda said to the Buddha: 'So it is, so it is;
it is truly as the Holy One has said,'" and below, Cunda extensively clarifies the preceding "Reality" (zhen) in response to Mañjuśrī;
3. From "The light shone upon Mañjuśrī," and below, the Buddha extensively clarifies the preceding "Response" (ying) in response to Cunda.

Regarding the first part of the preceding section: because Cunda presented his offering, it is clarified that the Buddha should accept it; yet in reality, he is without dependence and without differentiation, and is thus eternal.

Second, from "At that time, the great assembly heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for the sake of all... onwards, because Cunda requested him to remain, it is clarified that the Buddha should enter extinction; yet in reality, he does not undergo transition, and being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he is eternal.
In the first part of the middle section, Cunda’s request serves as the cause for briefly opening up the teaching on the eternal Dharma;
secondly, Cunda addresses the Buddha regarding the non-differentiation between the two kinds of giving;
and from the words "It is not so" onwards, Cunda’s posing of difficulties serves as the cause for extensively explaining the meaning of the eternal.
Within the first section, there is first the request and subsequently the response.
In the request, the individuals making the request are first identified and enumerated.
The phrase "At that time, within the assembly" indicates their location.
"There was an upāsaka" identifies that individual;
this was actually a great sage manifesting as a resident, guiding beginners beyond their reach.
"In the city of Kuśinagara" specifies his dwelling place.
"Son of a craftsman" indicates his lineage;
"named Cunda" specifies his personal name; "together with fifteen of his peers" enumerates his retinue.
Question: Are these the same upāsakas as those listed above?
Explanation:
"It is not so; how do you know it is not?
They have come from afar, and these are the original assembly.
Furthermore, the lay devotees (upāsakas) who were here before have already prepared the food and drink, which they offered to the Buddha, but he did not accept them."
Now, this Cunda had not yet made any formal arrangement; it was only after receiving the Buddha’s permission that he was finally able to prepare everything. Thus, we know they were not the same.
If he were not among the previous assembly, why would the old residents of Kuśinagara not have been listed in the preceding introduction?
Those not included are many; why single out this one for reproach?
The following serves as a formal request:

"In order to cause the world to obtain wholesome fruits. This refers to the skillful means of mental action (*manas-karman*); because the Bodhisattva’s compassion is profound, whatever he performs is not done except for the sake of sentient beings. Therefore, by making this offering now, he acts so that the world may obtain what is wholesome.
"Good" refers to wholesome causes, and its fruit is the fruit of happiness. Since Cunda offered [the food] himself, how could he cause the world to obtain wholesome fruits?
Because by making this offering he attains Buddhahood and transforms others to be like himself, he enables them to obtain it as well.
From "sacrificing the body" onwards is the application of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
There are four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*):
walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Now, setting aside his seated posture, he proceeds to where the Buddha is.
"Rising from his seat" manifests the sign of his departure;
"baring his right shoulder" indicates that there is a task to be performed.
Regarding "kneeling with the right knee on the ground," there are three interpretations:
first, the right knee possesses strength, such that kneeling provides stability;
second, the right knee possesses strength, making it easier to rise and sit.
Second, because the right side is generally more restless, one should bring it to rest by placing it on the ground.
Therefore, a practitioner of dhyāna should ensure that both the right hand and the right foot are positioned below.
"Joining the palms toward the Buddha" is for the purpose of concentrating the mind.
"Wailing and shedding tears" means seeking the Buddha’s compassion.
They weep out of pity for the world's long-standing suffering, grief that they themselves are submerged in it, and because the Buddha is departing. Thus, they wail.
"Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet" manifests the depth of one's own devotion.
The head is what one holds as most honorable, while the feet are the lowest part of the Buddha; by joining the honorable to the lowly, the utmost degree of reverence is revealed.
From "And he addressed the Buddha" onwards, his verbal speech constitutes the formal invitation; first, he invites [the Buddha] to accept the offerings.
From "As a kṣatriya... onwards, he requests the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
From "The offerings I now present, though meager... onwards, he again invites [the Buddha] to accept the offerings.
Because Cunda had previously offered a donation to the great assembly and the Tathāgata had not yet accepted it, he first requested permission to offer his own gift.
Having requested the gift for the sake of merit, he then requested the Dharma for the sake of seeking wisdom in accordance with the teaching.
Although we previously requested an offering, we feared that the Tathāgata would likewise refuse it as he did before; therefore, we have made this request again.
Within the previous request for an offering, the first part was for the sake of others, beginning with "From now on, we shall be without a master," while the second part was for our own sake.
Regarding the practice for others, the text first requests the acceptance of offerings and subsequently reveals the purpose; this is clear and easily understood.
Regarding the practice for oneself, the text first clarifies the purpose and subsequently requests the acceptance of offerings; such is the arrangement of the text.
In the middle section clarifying what is to be done, there are eight distinct points:
the first six concern the absence of persons, the next one concerns the absence of dharmas, and the last one concludes the request.
"From now on, there is no master" means there is no place from which to depart from evil.
Regarding the phrase "having no kin," it means there is no place to accumulate merit; since there were Buddhas previously, it is said that [the situation] begins from now.
"Having no rescue and no protection" clarifies the loss of a master: it shows there is no rescue for present evils and no protection against future evils.
"Having no refuge and no destination" clarifies the loss of kin: at the beginning there is nowhere to turn for refuge, and in the end there is nowhere to go.

These six beings are destitute, impoverished, and suffering from hunger; they lack wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*). Desiring to seek their future sustenance from the Tathāgata, they have bound themselves to this request, thinking that from now on they will have no masters or kin; thus, they seek their future sustenance from the Tathāgata.
Making offerings to the Buddha with the expectation of the fruit is called "seeking.
Because the future fruit of Buddhahood will relieve one's own lack and deprivation, it is metaphorically termed "food.
Furthermore, because the fruit of giving food in the present life arises from its cause, it is named "food" after that cause.
The preceding section clarifies that which is being done.
From "I only pray" (*vande*) onwards is the conclusion of the request to accept the offerings.
"Only" (*vande*) carries the sense of exclusivity; because one exclusively seeks the acceptance of the offerings, it is called "I only pray."
To enter extinction after the meal is called "subsequent nirvana.
Since Cunda’s present offering was not merely a presentation of alms, but was also intended as a request for [the Buddha] to remain, why do you say that he permitted the Buddha's nirvana midway?
Matters cannot be discussed simultaneously; first, please accept our offerings, and only after you have accepted them may we request that you remain.

Furthermore, as Cunda was making his final offering at the time of the Buddha’s impending parinirvāṇa, he was unable to request that the Buddha stay; had he requested that the Buddha remain, the Buddha could not have entered parinirvāṇa.

Following "Please the Buddha to accept this offering," next comes the invitation to the Dharma. The first part, from the beginning up to "to rescue and reach," is for one's own sake; the second part, from "and [others]" onwards, is for the sake of others.
These correspond respectively to the left and right sides mentioned previously.
Regarding the section on "for oneself," there is first the simile and then the application (*yoga*).
From "I only pray" onwards is the conclusion and the request for the teaching to be given.

Within the simile, there are six phrases: "Just as a Kṣatriya," and so forth, is the first phrase. This similes for one who seeks the Dharma for themselves—specifically a member of the Kṣatriya royal caste; the Brāhmaṇa refers to those of pure conduct and noble lineage; the Vaiśya refers to the middle class; and the Śūdra refers to those of miscellaneous labor. Among these four castes, any single type is cited as an example; the poor person is taken as the metaphor, rather than all four being included.
People say:
"I raise this as a request; if the Buddha preaches the Dharma, I shall be equal to the Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas;
if the Buddha does not preach it, I shall be equal to the Vaiśyas and Śūdras."
If that were so, would people in the world be able to become Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas simply by receiving rain from heaven, and become Vaiśyas and Śūdras by not receiving it?
In meaning, there is no such principle.
"Because of poverty" is the second phrase; it serves as a metaphor for what one currently lacks.
"Having traveled far to another [place]" and so forth is the third phrase; it serves as a metaphor for what was done in the past.

In the past, Cunda abandoned heterodoxy to return to the orthodox; because heterodoxy and orthodoxy are fundamentally different, this is called "being distant. His taking refuge in the Buddha-Dharma is called "reaching another land," and his practicing causes to support the fruit is called "performing labor."
The section beginning with "obtaining what is good" constitutes the fourth line, which serves as a metaphor for that which one already possesses.
The section beginning with "having no sand" constitutes the fifth line, which serves as a metaphor for that which one does not possess.
The phrase "only hoping for heaven" below constitutes the sixth line, which serves as a metaphor for what one seeks.
In the application (*yōjō*), the order is not sequential and it is also incomplete.
It first applies the latter three lines and then applies the former two; therefore, it is said to be "not sequential."
The third [case] is not consistent, and thus it is said that [the analogy] is not exhaustive.
First, the fourth is correlated.

Regarding the phrase "taming the ox," this reiterates the preceding metaphor; by correlating the seven [transgressions] of body and speech, it reveals the Dharma, thereby clarifying the existence of practice.
"Cunda had previously become a lay follower (*upāsaka*), having eliminated the three evils of the body and departed from the four faults of speech; these constitute the seven [precepts].
'The excellent field is level and even' reiterates the previous metaphor; this metaphor uses wisdom to manifest the Dharma, clarifying that there is understanding."
Cunda had previously cultivated a limited understanding, which could serve as a great cause; therefore, it is called a "field.
When correct understanding is not deviant, it is termed "level and upright.
As for "pervasive," this refers to the great understanding cultivated in the past, which is here named "wisdom."

Next, the fifth section, beginning with "There is no sand," etc., restates the preceding parable to illustrate the removal of afflictions (*kleśa*), thereby clarifying the Dharma through its application.

The view-afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*) that Cunda has previously severed are like that sand and salt-marsh; the cultivation-afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) he has severed are like the stumps and brushwood.
Furthermore, the four abodes (*catur-vihāra*) that are to be severed are like that saline soil, and what arises from these four abodes is like the stumps and brushwood.

From the words "World-Honored One" onwards corresponds to the sixth phrase; "I now possess a field for taming oxen within my body" cites the fourth phrase; "having removed the stumps and brushwood" cites the fifth phrase. These are cited because one seeks the Dharma by relying upon this [field].

From "only longing" (*kevalam ākāṅkṣanti*) onwards, this correctly corresponds to the sixth [verse]. "Tathāgata" corresponds to the sky, and "the nectar-like rain of Dharma" (*amṛtadharmavarṣa*) corresponds to the preceding rain.
Based on the metaphor, it is called the "Dharma," and it is named the "Nectar Rain."
"Belonging to the four castes" corresponds to the first phrase; "poor in the treasure of the Dharma" corresponds to the second phrase.
Having thus completed the correspondence, [the text continues with] "I only pray that you will take pity on me and sever my poverty," which is the formal request for the teaching to be given.
The preceding section explains acting for oneself; the following clarifies acting for others.
"To rescue" (zhěng) means to deliver.
Because he speaks of universal deliverance, it is called "rescuing immeasurable sentient beings from suffering and affliction."
The following section is a request for offerings.
"My offerings, though few" expresses humility regarding the meagerness of the offering;
as stated in the subsequent text, the rice amounted to only eight *shu*, hence it is described as "slight."
Although what is offered is meager, it is hoped that it may be extensively fulfilled; since a small amount can serve as a basis for much, he therefore says "although. Question:

Since Cunda’s offering below serves as an adornment for the Tathāgata’s dwelling place, making the three thousandfold world-system like the Land of Peace and Bliss, he ought to be capable of extensive eloquence; why then is his offering so slight?
The commentary states:

Cunda was indeed capable of extensive eloquence; however, wishing to entrust even a small portion [of his teaching] to manifest the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata and cause the assembly to take refuge with faith, the great multitude below beheld this supernatural transformation and all rejoiced greatly.
"May it suffice for the Tathāgata and the great assembly" expresses his broad intention; "jì" (冀) means "to hope.
He hopes that with this food the Buddha and the multitude will be satisfied, just as Vimalakīrti took a single bowl of rice hoping it would satisfy all.

One who speaks these words desires to enable the Tathāgata to fulfill his own heart's wish by expanding the small into the great, so that the great assembly may behold the Buddha’s supernatural transformations and rejoice with faith and delight.

From the passage "I am now without a master and without kin" onwards, he requests that the Buddha compassionately accept him; this reiterates the aforementioned lack of master or kin to entreat the Buddha’s pity, seeking the Buddha’s profound compassion and begging to be treated like Rāhula.
Rāhu was the son of the Buddha’s birth-body; his compassionate love for him was profound and heavy, and because he deeply pitied sentient beings, [the Buddha] often took him as an example.
Below, the Buddha answers him.
“At that time, the World-Honored One” introduces the person who provides the response.
"Omniscience, the unsurpassed tamer" enumerates the virtue of the response.
To know all phenomena in their various specific categories is called "all-knowledge"; to tame oneself and to tame others, being the ultimate among tamers, is called the "unsurpassed tamer."

In terms of their distinct meanings, the "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the quality of being a teacher; the "unsurpassed taming" is the quality of being worthy of offerings, for by having tamed one's own mind, one is able to receive the sustenance of others.

In terms of their common meaning, these qualities are equivalent: because of omniscience, one is able to preach the Dharma and receive offerings, while also knowing the proper time for preaching and the proper time for receiving;
because of unsurpassed taming, one is able to tame sentient beings, preaching the Dharma for them and receiving offerings from them.
The section beginning with "He addressed Cunda" clarifies the words of response. First, he generally praises the excellence of the matter requested, and thus says "Excellent.
The word "excellent" (*śobhana*) is an auxiliary particle; because the request is appropriate and timely, it is reiterated as a mark of praise.
The Buddha answered him directly, first granting permission to preach the Dharma and subsequently granting permission to accept the offerings.
Why does this sequence differ from the wording of the initial request?
It is because Cunda’s intention was solely to present the offerings; therefore, he requested that they be accepted first.
The Buddha’s intention lies in the Dharma; therefore, he first teaches the Dharma.

His statement, “I shall now eliminate your poverty for you,” corresponds to the request made above, “I only pray that out of compassion, you will eliminate my poverty. Because one attains the fruit through this teaching, poverty is eliminated; this clarifies that which is to be removed.

"The unsurpassed rain of Dharma shall fall upon the field of your body" responds to the request above to "only long for the rain of Dharma. Bestowing the Dharma based on the previous seven limbs of body and speech is called "raining upon your body"; bestowing the Dharma based on the previous excellent field of wisdom is called "raining upon your field."

Because the Dharma is designated by way of a metaphor as "rain," it is called "rain"; because it is taught that it gives rise to the seeds of the *dharmakāya*, it is called "producing the sprouts of the Dharma.
This clarifies what is bestowed.

Within the acceptance of offerings, the passage beginning with "You now desire long life from me" cites what is sought; the preceding section, "The food to come shall be your life-span," names that which was previously requested.
"I shall now speak" below is the formal acceptance of offerings; because the Buddha accepts these offerings, it enables others to attain their fruits, and for this reason it is called "giving.
Because one constantly plants merit in the field [of the Sangha], the resulting retribution does not fail to manifest, and for this reason it is called "constant."

Longevity, physical form, and so forth constitute the essence of its fruit; by giving food in the present, one enables the recipient to obtain these five benefits—longevity, physical form, strength, tranquility, and eloquence—and thus obtains this very fruit in the future.
The section beginning with "Why" provides the explanation, first posing a preliminary inquiry.
This question carries two intentions:
first, it asks about the cause of the practice—how one can personally attain the fruit—and second, it asks why I say, "I shall bestow this upon you."
The second question concerns the five fruits, which are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). For what reason do I say that I bestow upon you the eternal?
Below, this is explained in detail; first, the bestowal of the eternal is explained.
What is the intended meaning of this explanation?
Because the self is eternal, it can bestow eternity upon you.

However, in this present passage, we only explain the eternity of the Buddha; once the eternity of the Buddha is established, that [eternity of the self] is revealed of itself, without the need for further argumentation.
Question: Why not simply seek the realization of permanence attained by those [others] directly, rather than seeking it through the Buddha?
Explanation:
That [reality] is always to come but has not yet appeared; it is obscure and difficult to manifest, and thus is discussed in relation to the Buddha.

The Buddha is constantly obscured by his past provisional traces; now, it is necessary to sweep away the provisional in order to reveal the real. Therefore, he is manifested through the non-differentiation of these two periods.
He called out "Cunda" to inspire his mind.
There are two types of giving food, yet their karmic rewards do not differ; this is the correct understanding of the constant meaning.

Regarding the two ways of giving food, the text is brief and difficult to understand; if it were complete, it should state that there are two kinds of recipients of the gift of food. The translator, wishing to form a four-character phrase, omitted the initial word "receiving."
How is this known? It is because the following section distinguishes between two types based on the recipient.

If there were no difference in the fruit, it would merely negate the provisional to reveal the real; yet when discussing according to the transformative teachings, receiving the gift at the earlier time is the cause and not the fruit, while receiving the gift at the later time is the fruit and not the cause. This duality of cause and fruit constitutes impermanence.
According to reality, there is nothing that is not the fruit of Buddhahood during these two periods; since the retributive fruits do not differ, they are therefore permanent (*nitya*).

Question: Previously, it was stated that this section—based on Cunda’s offering—clarifies that the Buddha has no dependence, and thus he is called permanent. For what reason is permanence now explained through the absence of difference?
The commentary states:
"Non-differentiation" (wuchā) likewise means being without dependence; since neither the present nor the past time involves mutual dependence, it is called non-differentiation.
Below, the two characteristics are distinguished, first by posing a question and then by providing the analysis.

Regarding "First, having received [the offering], he attained Bodhi": prior to becoming a Buddha, he first accepted the milk-gruel offered by the two maidens, and only thereafter did he attain Buddhahood. *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is a foreign term; in this language, it means "Unsurpassed, Right, True, and Perfect Enlightenment."
"A" means "non-"; "nuttara" means "supreme"; "samyak" means "right"; "sambodhi" means "true. "Samyak" is further named "right," and "bodhi" is named "the Way."
"Second, having accepted it, one enters nirvana" refers to what is received now.
The preceding section explained "permanence"; the following explains the meaning of "giving.

"I now accept your final offering so that you may be fully endowed with *dāna*" refers to attaining the fruit in the future; therefore, it is called "giving. This is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), not any other kind of giving.
Above, by virtue of the request, the eternal Dharma was briefly elucidated.
From here on, the second section addresses Cunda’s posing of difficulties to extensively explain the meaning of the eternal.
Cunda first raises an objection regarding the statement of non-differentiation, contending that it contradicts what he had previously heard; therefore, he challenges it.
"The two types of giving and their karmic fruits, as taught by the Buddha, are not without distinction; it is not so," this serves as a general negation of the opponent's position.
"For what reason? and so forth, extensively demonstrates why it is not so.

First, I shall examine myself as to why I claim that the Buddha is not so; below, five points are raised as refutations to demonstrate that there is no difference [between us] and to establish the aforementioned "not so":

first, a refutation based on the field (*kṣetra*); second, based on the person (*pudgala*); third, based on the body (*kāya*); fourth, based on the cause (*hetu*); and fifth, based on the conditions (*pratyaya*).
Receiving offerings constitutes a field; therefore, one first addresses the field.
The field consists of persons; therefore, one next addresses the person.
A person must possess a physical body; therefore, one next refers to the body.
Since the body must have a basis, one next proceeds to the cause (*hetu*);
since the body has that which it relies upon, one next proceeds to the condition (*pratyaya*).
Within these five difficulties, there should accordingly be three [types of analysis]:

First, it demonstrates how the past differs from the present; second, it clarifies how the present differs from the past; and third, it concludes by showing that the refutation is without discrepancy. However, within the current text, there are instances where these points are complete and where they are incomplete.
Regarding the first field (*kṣetra*), only the first two [points] are present: First, demonstrating how the past differs from the present:

"The donor who previously received the gift had not yet exhausted their afflictions (*kleśa*)," meaning the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) was not perfected; "they had not yet achieved the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)," meaning the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) was not fully prepared; and "they were unable to cause others to give with full perfection," meaning the merit generated was not superior.

Second, it clarifies that the present is different from the past: "The recipient who later receives the gift has already exhausted his afflictions," which clarifies the perfection of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); "He has already perfected the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)," which clarifies the completeness of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); and "Causing [the donor] to be fully endowed with birth," which clarifies the excellence of merit produced;
third, the conclusion of the refutation should follow, but it is omitted in the text.
The second category of persons should likewise possess all three [characteristics], yet the text mentions only two:

first, the term "previously received" refers directly to sentient beings (*sattva*), indicating that their past state differs from the present. At the time they previously received the gift, their birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) was not yet exhausted; they were still encompassed by numerous cycles of birth and death, and are therefore called "sentient beings."
Second, the section beginning with "receiving [the fruit] later" clarifies that the present is different from the past. As explained in the following text, there are five kinds of devas:

first, the worldly devas (*laukika-deva*), which the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls "nominal devas. This refers to those whom the people of the world call "sons of heaven" (*devaputra*) or "kings of heaven" (*devendra*).
Second are the gods of birth, ranging from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception;
third are the pure gods, ranging from the *srotāpanna* up to the *pratyekabuddha*;

fourth are the gods of meaning, ranging from those on the first stage of the bodhisattva path up to those on the Dharma-cloud stage; because these various bodhisattvas understand and penetrate the meaning of emptiness, they are called "gods of meaning."

The fifth is the *paramārtha-deva* (Ultimate Truth Deity), referring to the Buddha-Tathāgata who has seen the nature of reality to its ultimate limit; he is named the *paramārtha-buddha*. Among these five types of deities, he is the supreme deity and is thus called the "Deity among Deities" (*devātideva*).
The three points regarding how it should be refuted are omitted from the text.

Within the section on the "refutation of the body," the full text contains three parts. First, it demonstrates the difference between the past and the present: "The recipient of the alms was a body of mixed food" explains the body in terms of conditions;
"the body of afflictions" explains the body in terms of causes, as it arises from afflictions and gives rise to afflictions.

Regarding the phrase “this is the final body, the impermanent body”: one distinguishes the body by its defining characteristics. “Final” (paścima) excludes what precedes it; as it is the ultimate limit of birth and death, it is called “final.
“Impermanent” (anitya) differs from the latter [the finality]; because the mechanism of transition has not yet ceased, it is named “impermanent.”
Second, it clarifies that the present is different from the past: "The recipient of the gift later possesses a body free from afflictions," which reverses the previous state of having afflictions.

Regarding the term "vajra" (diamond/thunderbolt), this is discussed separately and does not refer to a reversal of the former; rather, because his body is difficult to destroy, it is likened to a vajra.
“Dharmakāya” (法身) is the opposite of the aforementioned body of mixed food; because it is formed by the accumulation of all meritorious dharmas, it is called the Dharmakāya.
“Constant” (常) is the opposite of impermanent (無常), and “boundless” (無邊) is the opposite of having limits (邊).

Question: Cunda has already refuted the argument that [the Buddha] attains Buddhahood as something impermanent. Now, since it is stated that when the Tathāgata subsequently receives offerings, he possesses a Dharma-body, an eternal body, and an infinite body, it is already known that the Buddha is eternal; why then is there a need for further objection?
The commentary states:

When Cunda argues that the Buddha is permanent (*nitya*), he means that because he has attained the state of non-retrogression once and for all, he is called "permanent"; it does not mean he is immutable. Therefore, his argument is considered difficult to refute.

Alternatively, one might concede Cunda’s point that the Buddha is permanent yet differs from how he was in the past; however, since there is a difference between the present and the past, this remains impermanent (*anitya*). Such is the intent of the objection.
Third, from "How so? onwards, the refutation of the lack of distinction is concluded.
Within the section on the critique based on causes, there are also three parts:

first, to show that the past differs from the present, [the text states] "The one who previously received the gift was not yet endowed with *dāna*," etc., clarifying that his practice was not yet perfected.
The meaning of the six perfections is explained extensively in a separate chapter.
The phrase "only obtaining flesh" below indicates that his understanding is incomplete.
Why are the five eyes referred to as "understanding"?
Among the five eyes, the Buddha-eye, the wisdom-eye, and the dharma-eye are of the nature of cognitive understanding.
The meaning of the five eyes is also as explained in a separate chapter.
Among the five eyes, the flesh-eye is first, the deva-eye is second, the wisdom-eye is third, the dharma-eye is fourth, and the Buddha-eye is fifth.
Among these five, the fleshly eye exists prior [to the path], and thus it is said that one "only obtains" it;
the other four are produced through cultivation and have not yet been obtained at that time.
Within those not yet obtained, the divine eye—which is a mundane dharma—is now set aside and not discussed; the remaining three, which are noble wisdoms, are now being analyzed here.

Among these three [categories], one should speak from bottom to top as "not yet having attained the eye of wisdom up to the Buddha-eye. However, in this present passage, the order proceeds from top to bottom; therefore, it says "not yet having attained the Buddha-eye down to the eye of wisdom. The term "nai" (乃) signifies "transgressing" or "skipping" the established sequence of the dharma.
This is spoken according to the distinct teachings of the three vehicles; in reality, however, bodhisattvas also partially possess the five eyes.

Second, it clarifies how the present differs from the past: "The later recipient of the gift has already fulfilled dāna," and so forth, which clarifies the perfection of their practice, because these various pāramitās are cultivated by bodhisattvas and perfected by Buddhas.
The phrases "possessing the Buddha-eye" and so forth manifest the perfection of his realization.
Within the eyes of the sages, one proceeds from the highest downward; therefore, it says "possessing the Buddha-eye" down to the "wisdom-eye," while the divine and fleshly eyes are not considered.
Third, from "How so" onwards, the conclusion refutes the lack of distinction.
Within the section on the difficulty regarding conditions, there are also three parts:
first, the statement "Previously it was received, entered the abdomen, and digested," etc., demonstrates that the past was different from the present.
Second, from "receiving [the fruit] later" onwards, it clarifies that the present is different from the past.
Regarding "lacking the five fruits," this means lacking the five types of results produced by food, namely: form, strength, longevity, and so forth.
3. From "How so? onwards, the conclusion establishes that there is no difference [in the merit].

Below, the Buddha explains the objection; this does not follow the sequence of the questions. First, he establishes the lack of difference with respect to the person; second, with respect to the cause; third, with respect to the individual; fourth, with respect to the field; and fifth, with respect to the conditions.
The body is the substance of virtue; therefore, one first attends to it.
The body must have a source; therefore, one next attends to its cause.
The body can become a person; therefore, one next attends to the person.
Because the body is capable of receiving offerings, one next proceeds to the field;
because the body has dependencies, one next proceeds to the conditions.
Within these five categories, there should likewise be three [aspects] by analogy.
First, it clarifies that the past is identical to the present; second, it clarifies that the present is identical to the past; third, it concludes by establishing their non-differentiation.

However, within the current text, there is an inequality regarding presence and absence: in the first section, only the first of these three points exists, while the latter two sentences are absent, which is evident from the text itself.
The second cause should likewise possess all three [aspects], yet the text contains only the first and the third, omitting the second.
Furthermore, within the initial section, the resolution of the objection is not exhaustive.
Why is it said that this is not exhaustive?

In the previous refutation, it was stated that if one first accepts offerings, the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) will not be complete and the five eyes (pañcacakṣus) will be insufficient. Now, however, only the eyes are explained while the six perfections are not discussed;
furthermore, among the five eyes, only the Buddha-eye (buddhacakṣus) is explained while the other four are not. Therefore, it is said to be not exhaustive.
Since this single principle is thus established, other similar cases may be understood accordingly; therefore, they are not explained in detail.
How is it known that this is a partial explanation of the Buddha-eye?
It is because the illumination and vision of the Buddha-nature constitutes the Buddha-eye.

In the text, the initial statement, "That which has not yet seen the Buddha-nature is called the body of afflictions and the body of mixed food," etc., clarifies the reality by means of the preceding [phenomena]; it may also be termed clarifying the cause by means of the fruit.
How is this manifested?
That which has not yet seen the Buddha-nature is called the body of afflictions (*kleśakāya*), because it is a body that consumes mixed food, is subject to its final limit, and is impermanent.

Since it was previously proclaimed that for immeasurable kalpas there has been no body of food or body of afflictions, it is clearly known that I have already seen the Buddha-nature throughout immeasurable kalpas; and because the nature has been seen, the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) existed prior to that.

The passage beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva received food and drink" explains the phenomenal manifestation (nirmāṇakāya) in relation to the ultimate reality (dharmatā). How is this manifested?

In truth, the Tathāgata has already possessed the eternal body and has already realized the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu) since immeasurable kalpas ago; yet, to say that "at that time, having received food and drink, he entered the Vajra-samādhi and only then saw the Buddha-nature and attained bodhi" clearly demonstrates that [the former state] was a phenomenal manifestation.

The passage beginning with "Therefore, I" concludes that there is no difference, precisely because the nature of reality (dharmatā) was seen identically both then and now; thus, the two fruits are without distinction.
Within the third person, the text contains three parts:
first, the statement "At that time, he destroyed the four Māras" demonstrates that the past is identical to the present.
The afflictions, the aggregates, death, and the celestial Māra—these are the four. By destroying the affliction-māra, one leaves behind the cause of birth and death;

by destroying the celestial māra, one leaves behind the conditions for birth and death; by destroying the aggregates and death, one leaves behind the fruit of birth and death. Because these four māras are destroyed, one is no longer a sentient being.
Second, from "Now entering" onwards, it clarifies that the present is the same as the past.
Third, from "Therefore" onwards, it concludes by establishing their non-differentiation.
Within the fourth section on the field (*kṣetra*), there are likewise three parts:
The initial statement, “At that time, although it was not extensive,” and so forth, demonstrates that the past is identical to the present, thereby resolving the objection incompletely.

Previously, the objection was raised: “The former recipients of the gift had not yet exhausted their afflictions, had not yet attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), and were thus unable to cause others to fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). However, here the response is direct: as long as there is wisdom, the purpose is fulfilled; nothing else need be discussed.

This clarifies that although the Tathāgata did not extensively expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures at the time he previously received offerings, he had already thoroughly mastered them; therefore, I am one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom.
The twelve divisions of the scriptures will be fully explained below.
Second, from "Now entering" onwards, it clarifies that the present is the same as the past.
Third, from "Therefore" onwards, it concludes by establishing their non-differentiation.
